Before you leave

Most plants can go a week without attention if you set them up well the day before. Water everything thoroughly, move plants out of direct sun and away from radiators or heating vents, and group them together — a cluster of pots keeps the air around them more humid than a single pot on a sill. Lower the thermostat a little if you can; cooler rooms dry out slower.

Do not fertilize or repot in the days before a trip. Both push growth and raise water demand at exactly the wrong time.

  • Water deeply the day before, then let the pots drain so nothing sits in a full saucer.
  • Move sun-lovers a few feet back from south or west windows; they will cope with less light for two weeks.
  • Group thirsty plants on trays of damp pebbles or in the bathroom, where humidity is highest.
  • Check for pests before you go — a small infestation becomes a large one in two unattended weeks.

What to tell your plant sitter

Write less than you think. A sitter will follow 'half a cup from the top, let it drain' far more reliably than a paragraph about the plant's history. Put the plants that genuinely need attention at the top of the sheet, mark the ones that should be ignored entirely (most succulents), and leave the watering can and a measuring cup next to the sheet. If a plant is precious, say so — and say what to do if it looks unhappy, which is usually 'wait, do not water more'.

Strategy by trip length

What works when, for an average collection of houseplants in a home that stays at normal room temperature.

Away forMost houseplantsThirsty plants (ferns, calathea, peace lily)Succulents & cacti
Up to 5 daysWater well before leaving; no other actionWater well, move away from heat, tray of damp pebblesNothing — do not water before leaving if soil is still moist
1–2 weeksWater well; move out of direct sun; most will be fine, a few may droop and recoverSelf-watering: wick from a water reservoir, bottle spike, or set the pot in the bath on a wet towelNothing; many go 3–4 weeks
2–4 weeksA sitter every 7–10 days with this sheet, or wicks and reservoirs for each potA sitter at least weekly; wicks alone are risky this longOne watering around the midpoint is plenty
Over a monthA sitter with this sheet, or move plants to someone's homeA sitter; consider a timer-driven drip systemA sitter every 3–4 weeks

Self-watering methods — wicks, spikes, globes — deliver water unevenly. Test them for a few days before you leave so you know which pots they keep too wet or too dry.

How to use this sheet

  1. Print the PDF a few days before you leave and fill it in while walking through the house plant by plant.
  2. Under How to water, be specific: 'about 1 cup from the top until it drains' or 'fill the saucer, empty after 20 minutes'.
  3. Work out the dates each plant falls due during the trip from its usual interval, and write only those dates.
  4. Note which plants to move out of direct sun before you leave, and which are deliberately on a no-water list.
  5. Leave the sheet with the watering can and a measuring cup where the sitter will see it.

Questions

Is this sheet really free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print — no sign-up, no email, no watermark.

How long can houseplants go without water?

Most tropical foliage plants in normal room conditions manage one to two weeks after a thorough watering, especially moved out of direct sun. Ferns and calathea may struggle past a week; succulents and cacti are fine for three or four weeks.

Should I water plants more before a trip to make up for it?

Water thoroughly, but once. Soil can only hold so much; a second heavy watering just leaves the pot sitting wet, which harms roots faster than a dry spell.

Do self-watering globes and spikes work?

They help for one to two weeks but deliver unevenly — fast in porous soil, barely at all in compacted mix. Test them before you go and prefer a human for longer trips.
